parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Let's make it smaller. What was the first thing you did when you started your last shift?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: That's fine. In your own words, what does your job as a dispatcher involve?

Q4
The answer just before it: As a dispatcher, I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way before signing off a flight before it leaves. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight. I also want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, though I know software never chooses a drone or a way for us.
The question: You mentioned that several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones. Can you tell me about a recent time when that happened?

The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Who are the other dispatchers planning alongside you — are they from your own company, or from others?

The question: Think back over the last few months. Was there a day that went especially badly?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You said software never chooses a drone or a way for you. Why does that matter to you?

Q10
The answer just before it: Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher. Because of this policy, software never chooses a drone or a way for us.
The question: You also said you want help finding out which of your drones could get to where a job starts. How do you find that out today?

The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You mentioned you can call off a flight. What would make you call one off?

The question: What worries you about a new service being introduced for your work?

Q13
The answer just before it: The service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and it occasionally crashes. I also worry because radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Furthermore, links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, so an instruction might get through twice while the sender cannot tell if the first attempt arrived.
The question: When an instruction to a drone might have got through twice, what could that lead to in your work?

Q14
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When reports from one of your drones stop arriving or come in late, what do you need to know first?

Q15
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You said the server is restarted during working hours while drones are flying. What happens to your work when that occurs?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What information about your flights would you not want other companies using the service to see?

Q17
The answer just before it: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, but that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
The question: How does airspace information reach you today, and who gives it to you?

Q21
The answer just before it: Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company. Furthermore, drones of several models have different charging connectors that are not interchangeable.
The question: When you and another dispatcher in your company want the same drone or charging pad at the same time, what happens?

The question: After you sign off a flight and it leaves, who is responsible for it next?

The question: Who are the people on the ground supervising the drones during flight?

Q27
The answer just before it: Drones are of several models from different manufacturers, differing in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, and which sensors they carry. Choosing the drone is my legal responsibility, and they also differ in which charging connector they use.
The question: At the moment you choose a drone for a job, what do you need to know about it?

Q28
The answer just before it: I need to know how much the drone can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, and which sensors it carries. I also need to know which charging connector it uses, and that choosing the drone is my legal responsibility.
The question: How do you know how much battery a drone actually has before a job?
